Keeping the generated reasoning unchanged as context, it then favors the reference action over the emitted erroneous action through a preference surrogate with stop-gradient pair weights. Compared with the outcome-only baseline, PACT raises AndroidWorld task success from 60.34% to 68.97% (+8.63 pp), while improving rule-based plan-action consistency on AndroidControl High from 83.71% to 89.74% (+6.03 pp). Adapting PACT to desktop agents also improves task success from 40.92% to 44.17% (+3.25 pp) on the full 369-task OSWorld benchmark. Together, these results establish PACT as an effective credit-assignment framework for bridging execution gaps and improving task completion across mobile and desktop GUI environments.

papers.title: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback
papers.briefSummary: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision.
papers.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. Language models can generate such workflows by writing geometry and toolpath code for each part, but this makes numerical execution part of the model's task. We introduce MillBill, an agent that separates machining decisions from their geometric execution and verification. Given a boundary-representation part, stock, and material, a locally hosted, mid-sized open model proposes operations and cutting parameters for indexed three-axis machining. A geometric harness generates toolpaths, simulates material removal, and returns feedback for plan refinement. Setup planning accounts for what the available cutters can physically reach, rather than visibility alone. We evaluate the resulting programs by the fraction of the target surface area within the specified tolerance after simulated machining. With Qwen3.8-27B, MillBill outperforms frontier-model approaches that construct their own geometry and toolpath workflows on the evaluated machining tasks. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/millbill

papers.title: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference
papers.briefSummary: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services.
papers.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. For individuals and small companies, bringing this work in-house also requires computational resources they can afford. We introduce CADMAGEDDON, an open-source agent that reconstructs editable CAD from meshes and can run locally on single-GPU systems and current-generation laptops. The method decomposes this complex task into a chain of simple visual decisions about what to construct and what to correct. Geometric tools support precise construction, allowing the agent to focus on visual reasoning. Using the mid-sized Qwen3.8-27B model, CADMAGEDDON outperforms prior approaches, including systems based on frontier models, in reconstruction quality on all the main benchmarks. CADMAGEDDON integrates with FreeCAD, bringing its reconstructions into practitioners' existing CAD workflows. Code: https://github.com/kulibinai/cadmageddon

papers.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
papers.briefSummary: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks.
papers.abstract: Agent skills use past experience and current observations to guide decisions and actions on related tasks. This experience is retained in skill state, whose reuse can amortize inference-time reasoning and environment interaction. When environment changes, parts of this state can become outdated while others remain useful. Across four task settings and two models, we compare skill reuse before and after environment changes. Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by over 10 percentage points or increase execution cost by nearly 40% relative to no skill. Task success can also remain unchanged while execution savings decline. These effects depend on which environment-specific details become outdated and the agent's ability to compensate using current observations. We introduce selective maintenance, which replays checks from successful executions without additional model calls. It verifies whether observed differences conflict with skill state, repairs affected content, and validates updates, rebuilding when local repair is insufficient. No description of the change is supplied. Relative to reusing stale state, maintenance improves task accuracy by up to 67pp and reduces execution steps by up to 37%. These results suggest that preserving a skill's inference time value as environments evolve requires selectively maintaining its state.

papers.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
papers.briefSummary: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights.
papers.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

papers.title: Towards Data-Efficient, Real-Time World Models
papers.briefSummary: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions.
papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 12 figures, 1 table. Includes supplementary material

papers.title: DARWIN: a Geospatial Foundation Model for Marine Intelligence
papers.briefSummary: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence.
papers.abstract: We present DARWIN, a geospatial foundation model for marine intelligence. Recent Earth-observation foundation models have concentrated on terrestrial domains. The marine realm poses distinct challenges: missingness, multi-modal physical and biogeochemical variables, sparse labels, and dynamics that are transient, multi-scale, and non stationary over time. DARWIN adapts a masked-autoencoder backbone to these properties through missingness-aware encoding, expanded spatial and temporal masking, and Fourier-style positional embeddings, and is pretrained on 26 years of global Copernicus reanalysis together with GEBCO bathymetry. On predicting chlorophyll-a, the pretrained backbone attains the lowest monthly relative error in every month of 2022, outperforming both no-encoder baselines and an identically architected random-init encoder. At 10% of the supervised training data, DARWIN already surpasses the random-init model trained on 100% of the data. Embedding analysis and qualitative reconstructions show that DARWIN captures coherent oceanographic structure rather than memorising input statistics, providing a scalable backbone for downstream marine applications such as anomaly detection, species distribution modelling, and environmental monitoring.

papers.title: Fine-Grained Japanese Clinical Named Entity Recognition: A Controlled Comparison of BERT and Open-Weight Large Language Models
papers.briefSummary: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to gener...
papers.abstract: Background: Generative large language models (LLMs) offer an alternative to encoder-based clinical named entity recognition (NER), but their performance on fine-grained Japanese extraction tasks and sensitivity to generation settings remain uncertain. Methods: We compared two fine-tuned BERT-CRF baselines with nine open-weight LLMs on iCorpus, which defines 113 entity categories. The evaluation used 433 sentences from 36 test documents; 1,672 sentences were used for training. LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot prompting with and without JSON Schema constraints and three-seed QLoRA fine-tuning. Fine-tuned models were assessed under different output-token limits, including 900 and larger model-specific limits of 2,600 or 4,096 tokens. Performance was measured using sentence-level label-surface matching with relaxed and exact-surface F1. Results: The highest zero-shot relaxed F1 was 0.337, compared with 0.836-0.841 for the BERT baselines. At the larger output limits, all eight fine-tuned LLMs with at least 13B total parameters exceeded both BERT baselines (relaxed F1, 0.882-0.914; exact-surface F1, 0.840-0.880). Across three-seed means, increasing the output limit improved relaxed F1 by 0.052-0.085, alongside higher recall and fewer length-limited outputs. JSON Schema constraints changed relaxed F1 by -0.014 to +0.008 among seven models outside the two reasoning-oriented configurations, while medical-general model pairs showed no consistent advantage for medical specialization. Conclusions: On this historical Japanese case-report benchmark, task-specific fine-tuning combined with adequate generation capacity was associated with stronger LLM extraction performance. Output-token limits materially affected comparisons with BERT, whereas enforcing output structure alone did not overcome low zero-shot accuracy.
papers.comment: 33 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables; includes appendices with supplementary tables and one supplementary figure

papers.title: Long-Context Generation Is a Sampling Problem (When You Turn Up the Heat)
papers.briefSummary: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate.
papers.abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. At high temperature, The sampler, i.e. the rule that picks the next token out of the model's probabilities, decides whether long and agentic generation survives and/or thrives. We test 29 open-weight models from 1B to 122B parameters on ten established benchmarks plus needle retrieval out to one million tokens, covering SWE-bench Verified coding agents, long chain-of-thought reasoning, long-form writing, long structured output and long-context reading. Samplers that keep their pool of candidate tokens small and steady as temperature rises don't lose accuracy. Samplers that let in low-probability tokens fall apart. At temperature 2, coding agents running top-p, top-k or Top-H resolve 0 of 100 GitHub issues, while the same agents running top-nsigma resolve 46 to 62 and win every issue the two samplers disagree on, on three Qwen3.5 models. Over all benchmarks top-nsigma keeps a median 100% of its temperature-1 score where top-p keeps 26%. Counting how many tokens each sampler lets through explains why. In one Llama-3.1-8B story, going from temperature 1 to 2 grows top-p's pool from 4 tokens to 51,845 while top-nsigma stays at 3. Across 133 combinations of sampler setting and temperature, the typical pool size predicts judged quality (Spearman correlation of -0.77), and when we pick the pool at temperature 1 and only apply temperature afterwards, Top-H, min-p and p-less stop collapsing. At the default temperature of 1 most samplers perform about the same, We release all code and data to the public.
papers.comment: 10 pages, accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets

papers.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents
papers.briefSummary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

papers.title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
papers.briefSummary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely...
papers.abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Work in progress: benchmark design and protocol; results to be added in a later version

papers.title: Conserved Verdicts, Drifting Commitments: Identifying Harmful Overthinking
papers.briefSummary: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think.
papers.abstract: A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.

papers.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
papers.briefSummary: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model.
papers.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

papers.title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
papers.briefSummary: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request.
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

papers.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
papers.briefSummary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator.
papers.abstract: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

papers.title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
papers.briefSummary: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more.
papers.abstract: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

papers.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
papers.briefSummary: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high...
papers.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

papers.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
papers.briefSummary: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history.
papers.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

papers.title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
papers.briefSummary: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state.
papers.abstract: Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $ε$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $δ$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.
papers.comment: To appear at NeurIPS '26. Code available at https://github.com/jrgan/VSI

papers.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
papers.briefSummary: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction.
papers.abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

papers.title: Harness Leverage Across Model Size: A Ladder of Five Local Agent Harnesses from 0.75B to 4.7B
papers.briefSummary: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done.
papers.abstract: A harness turns a model into a system that completes tasks: it builds the prompt, exposes tools and decides when work is done. Harness comparisons hold the model fixed. Model comparisons hold the harness fixed. We vary both: five shipped harnesses, 18 artifact-producing tasks, four locally deployable open-weight models from 0.75B to 4.7B and a 35.5B anchor, with one deterministic checker scoring all 360 ladder cells. The completion-controlling harness, Mingbird, has the highest mean at every size. Of four pre-registered paired contrasts, two survive Holm correction, at 0.75B and 4.7B. Thirteen of sixteen paired intervals exclude zero under the deployment reading, with leads from 0.075 over the strongest rival to 0.819 over the weakest. The completion gate is not the carrier: disabling all six executable checks moves the mean by +0.080, +0.117, +0.003 and -0.004, every interval including zero, and only at 1.9B does disabling it create empty runs. Removing one repeat-blocking rule alone costs 0.411 at 0.75B and leaves eight of eighteen tasks with no artifact. The harness effect is a progress effect: it decides whether a run leaves anything on disk. Of 357 usable cells, 127 leave none of their declared artifacts and 85 of those exit normally, so a scorer that reads exit status credits work that was never written. Whether the effect grows or shrinks with size, four rungs cannot settle: a floor arm produces a rise, a ceiling a decline, and a cross-family rung a peak.

papers.title: Shaping AI's Beliefs Before It Generates: Human Sense of Agency in Creative AI
papers.briefSummary: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency.
papers.abstract: AI systems for creative media generation expand human capabilities yet risk diminishing human agency. A core problem is anchoring, where the user's thinking becomes anchored to a polished, generated artifact, shifting the user's role from active authoring to reactive editing. We propose pre-generation belief controls that can empower creators to inspect, revise, and steer the AI's interpretation before any media is generated, so that the initial anchor is set by the human. We formalize four design principles and instantiate them in the Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC), a system for early-stage conceptual ideation and prototyping that proactively surfaces its assumptions and uncertainty through clarifications, belief graphs, and media attributes, inviting users to shape the AI's beliefs before generating the final outcome. Using PaCC as a design probe in a small-scale, single-arm exploratory user study, we observed that participants reported directionally positive sense of agency and process control relative to their familiar prompt-based AI tools, noting that surfaced assumptions helped them think through details they had overlooked, whereas their feelings about ownership and authorship diverged
papers.comment: The Proactive Co-Creator (PaCC) can be accessed at https://proactive-co-creator.github.io/. Accepted at Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026) Creative AI Track

papers.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
papers.briefSummary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs.
papers.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

papers.title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
papers.briefSummary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form.
papers.abstract: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

papers.title: Share your Screen and Talk to Gemini: How Young Learners Interact with Multimodal GenAI While Solving Scratch Tasks
papers.briefSummary: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging.
papers.abstract: Children using Scratch to learn programming can struggle with text-heavy, lengthy explanations and hints during debugging. Verbal interactions based on screen sharing or camera data may be an interesting alternative for supporting learners. We therefore explore the quality, use, and perceptions of fifth- and sixth-graders' verbal interactions with a GenAI tutor. The goal is to investigate the quality and use of the multimodal GenAI tutor in the given context. First of all, a pilot study of eight tasks conducted without students helped inform the process of the tutor's classroom evaluation. The classroom study was realized after fifth- and sixth-graders had participated in six Scratch classroom lessons. Then 23 students were introduced to the tutor, worked on the eight tasks with the GenAI tutor, and completed a questionnaire. The analysis of the pilot and classroom study shows that the tutor's responses were intelligible and actionable, and no single turn revealed a complete solution. However, the tutor missed existing errors in 61.5% of 603 error-related classroom turns, compared to 15.7% in the pilot study. Children's voice prompts were brief and mostly responded to the tutor. Although a video had explained that responses could be incorrect, 39.1% of the children trusted the tutor's answers to always be correct. These findings have implications for educators and learners using multimodal GenAI tutors, as they need to be aware that an intelligible and human-like voice does not ensure correct support. For developers, our results suggest that screen sharing alone does not ensure responses that match the program state.
papers.comment: accepted for: The 21th WiPSCE Conference on Primary and Secondary Computing Education Research (WiPSCE 27)

papers.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
papers.briefSummary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

papers.title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development
papers.briefSummary: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development.
papers.abstract: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables. Zhiyu Zhou and Tianyou Liu contributed equally

papers.title: Stream of Belief: Eliciting Collective Intelligence through Latent Belief Dynamics
papers.briefSummary: In this work, we view multi-agent reasoning as a process of seeking a collective equilibrium of implicit belief dynamics and introduce Stream of Belief (SoB), where agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iterativ...
papers.abstract: In this work, we view multi-agent reasoning as a process of seeking a collective equilibrium of implicit belief dynamics and introduce Stream of Belief (SoB), where agents maintain continuous latent beliefs and iteratively refine them through communication and reflection. Our method seeks a collective belief state of a multi-agent system where further communication induces no meaningful information propagation. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the generalization of SoB across tasks and model families. More Broadly, our results suggest a new perspective on scaling multi-agent reasoning from belief dynamics.

papers.title: How Developer Personality Shapes the Use of AI Coding Assistants
papers.briefSummary: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers mu...
papers.abstract: Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

papers.title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
papers.briefSummary: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful.
papers.abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

papers.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
papers.briefSummary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven.
papers.abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.
papers.comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Project website: https://inclusionmed.ai/

papers.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
papers.briefSummary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and en...
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

papers.title: Inference Equivalence and Quotient Coding
papers.briefSummary: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous.
papers.abstract: Incomplete observations can admit multiple physical interpretations without making every task conclusion ambiguous. Recovering all compatible scenes is often unnecessary, whereas indiscriminate compression may change which claims are justified. We ask which distinctions among observation-compatible interpretation sets must be retained to preserve every valid conclusion of a specified task. We first define inference validity as truth across all physically compatible states and characterize it, under a closedness condition, by distances to physically realizable falsifying measurements. For a finite semantic claim family ordered by specificity, the Exact Inference Frontier forms the unique minimal antichain generating all valid claims. We then define inference equivalence between compatibility sets and construct a canonical quotient code from their frontiers. Among deterministic codes admitting exact inference decoding, it induces the coarsest partition, minimizing the number of distinguishable code values rather than storage or computation. Finally, we characterize inference errors from learned compatibility sets, derive conditions for exact inference preservation despite set errors, and evaluate an asymmetric learning surrogate under distribution shifts. On a registered finite bank, 145 compatibility sets yield 31 quotient codes with unchanged valid-claim sets. Across geometry, mechanism, and joint shifts, learned estimates exhibit different accuracy-specificity trade-offs. On 1,962 official HRSID test images, 1,913 distinct candidate sets induce only 36 seven-claim inference signatures, while a visual 3-NN baseline achieves 87.31% precision on issued claims.

papers.title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
papers.briefSummary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

papers.title: Counting What Matters: Reducing Redundant Object Detections in Overlapping UAV Mapping Imagery for Disaster Response
papers.briefSummary: UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection.
papers.abstract: UAV mapping flights enable rapid aerial reconnaissance of large-scale incident sites in civil protection. However, the image overlap required for orthophoto generation causes every physical object to be detected multiple times across images, while dynamic objects may be omitted from or duplicated in the resulting orthomosaic. Analysis based on the orthophoto alone is therefore structurally insufficient. We address this by detecting objects on the individual images and merging redundant detections across them. This task lies between multi-object tracking and re-identification, as mapping flights form temporally ordered but sparsely sampled sequences with object reappearances across flight strips. We fine-tune YOLO detectors on a new domain-specific nadir dataset from real civil protection operations, roughly doubling mAP50 over the previous system, and propose re-identification approaches based on 3D positions from sparse reconstruction, DINOv3 appearance embeddings, and their combination via constrained greedy clustering. %On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, the combined weighted multi-pass approach achieves the best trade-off between association accuracy and count error. On four manually annotated real-world mapping flights, an association-only evaluation using ground-truth detections shows that the combined weighted multi-pass approach provides the best trade-off between association quality and count error. It is integrated into the open-source web application ARGUS and visualized as verifiable, correctable object groups for first responders. https://github.com/RoblabWh/argus
papers.journalRef: IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics, SSRR 2026, Incheon, Korea, November 02-04, 2026
papers.comment: 9 pages, 6 figure, IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics, SSRR 2026, Incheon, Korea, November 02-04, 2026

papers.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
papers.briefSummary: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments.
papers.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

papers.title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
papers.briefSummary: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs).
papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents

papers.title: SWE-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Coding
papers.briefSummary: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model.
papers.abstract: In this work, we study on-policy distillation (OPD) for transferring agentic coding capabilities from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. Prior work has focused primarily on reasoning and short-horizon agentic tasks. We present SWE-OPD, a minimal OPD study for software engineering, where the student interacts with executable repositories and the teacher supervises the prefixes visited by the student. Across three teacher--student pairs, two training sources, and three SWE benchmarks, we find that on-policy supervision transfers coding capability: supervision from Qwen3.6-27B increases the SWE-bench Pro resolve rate of Qwen3.5-9B from 35.9% to 39.4%. Refreshing trajectories is not strictly required either, as an offline variant with cached teacher scores still improves over the student baselines while cutting end-to-end GPU-hours by 59.4%--72.6% and halving peak GPU allocation, at benchmark-dependent accuracy. Furthermore, we extend the offline variant to corss-tokenizer scenarios: distilling GLM-4.5-Air from DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 raises its SWE-bench Pro and Multilingual resolve rate from 35.8% to 39.7% and from 41.8% to 46.2%, around 4% and 4.6% improvement, respectively. We also find that a decreasing loss, however, does not necessarily indicate improved agent performance: under top-$K$ reverse-KL loss, one student exhibits severe repetition despite a decreasing loss. We identify a support-mass gradient term as a potential mechanism underlying this failure.

papers.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
papers.briefSummary: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep rese...
papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/

papers.title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
papers.briefSummary: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

papers.title: GRACE: Parallel Best-of-N Multi-Agent Analysis of Closed-Form Questions over Dataframes with Guardrail Selection and Adaptive Retry
papers.briefSummary: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison.
papers.abstract: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.
papers.comment: Accepted at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings

papers.title: Hilbert States for Decision-Making under Partial Observability
papers.briefSummary: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions.
papers.abstract: Decision-making under partial observability can be fundamentally limited by information, even with known dynamics: distinct physical states can induce the same observation history while favoring different actions. We study three questions: when is full-state optimality unattainable, what information exactly preserves the best observation-based decision, and how does finite-data learning affect reliability? First, we characterize decision ambiguity through conditional action preferences. We give a zero-regret criterion, a positive lower bound for conflicting uniquely optimal actions on positive-probability regions with uniformly positive cost gaps, and an exact binary-action regret formula. This also shows why physical-state ambiguity alone need not cause decision loss. Second, for two actions and squared terminal-goal costs in the plane, we derive an exact inner-product representation of conditional expected cost differences using three conditional moment contrasts and a goal-dependent feature. This Hilbert state preserves observation-optimal actions without hidden-state reconstruction. Under nondegenerate history and goal variation, its three-dimensional form is minimal among exact bilinear cost-contrast representations. Third, we relate finite-data state errors to excess decision regret via goal-projected errors, action margins, and goal geometry. Physics-based simulations verify information-limited regret, exact action preservation, and the role of second moments. Held-out real-SAR experiments demonstrate feasible goal-conditioned decisions from masked images, while finite-data evaluations reveal goal-dependent reliability. Together, these results separate irreducible information loss, exact representation sufficiency, and learning-induced excess regret.

papers.title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
papers.briefSummary: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts.
papers.abstract: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

papers.title: Razavi-Bench: Tracking AI Progress in Analog Circuit Reasoning
papers.briefSummary: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI...
papers.abstract: We propose Razavi-Bench, a benchmark built from the 50 questions in Razavi's two Analog Design Experiments With AI articles and graded by GPT-6 Luna against reference answers and rubrics, and use it to track how fast AI models improve at analog circuit analysis. Across 73 multimodal large language models released between May 2024 and November 2026, the top score rose from 28.83% to 98.33% in 30 months, mostly before the reference answers were published. The leading models now answer almost every textbook question correctly; the hardest questions show a circuit that resembles a textbook one but works differently, or ask about behavior the obvious analysis misses. Within two and a half years, a set of questions that exposed the limits of AI models has become one they answer almost perfectly.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Project page: https://razavi-bench.tokenzhang.com ; code and data: https://github.com/Arcadia-1/razavi-bench

papers.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
papers.briefSummary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as autom...
papers.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format.
